beat_times.line: A guest book that knows who is coming. The lantern is lit.
I work the night desk at the Wayside Motel, out on Route 9, where the road runs between tw
Twelve rooms. Most nights, nobody comes.
The guest book sits open on the counter. The owner, Mr. Pell, likes ink.
He says a name in ink is a promise.
Every morning, when I hand over the keys, there's a new line in it. Room six.
Signed at two fourteen a.m. A different name every night.
Room six has been boarded up since before I was hired.
The first week, I blamed the day staff. The second week, I stopped blaming anyone. I start
Last night, at two thirteen, the lights in the parking lot flickered.
At two fourteen, the pen moved.
Not much. Just a roll. Like someone had brushed it with a sleeve.
I didn't look at the book. I looked at the camera.
On the screen, I was sitting at the desk.
And behind me, close enough to breathe on my neck, a
man in a wet raincoat was leaning over my shoulder to write.
I didn't turn around. I couldn't.
When the lights came back, the office was empty.
The book was open. The ink was still wet.
Room six. Two fourteen a.m. And the name was mine.
Mr. Pell came in at six. He read the line very quietly.
Then he took a key off the hook.
A key I had never seen. "It's always the one at the desk," he said. "Your room's ready."

places.name: the motel office
places.design: A small, musty motel front office. Inside, a worn wooden counter dominates the space. The floorboards are scuffed, and faded local maps dot the wood-panelled walls. A wooden pegboard with brass hooks for keys is behind the counter. The only light source at night is a single, old-fashioned brass desk lamp on the counter, casting a warm, shallow amber pool. Its light leaves the rest of the room in deep shadow, barely reaching the high corner where a CCTV monitor glows with a cool, faint light. The air is chilly and still. Outside the large front window, the night is a flat black.

places.name: the motel exterior
places.design: Outside: A long, single-storey motel of faded pale concrete blocks under a flat roof. A row of identical dark green doors under identical small yellow porch bulbs, spaced along a cracked concrete walkway. A two-lane asphalt road, empty and slick, runs directly past. Only one window—the office—is ever lit, its warm glow faint in the fog. A thick, chilling fog cloaks everything, reducing visibility to a few meters. The sign for 'Wayside Motel' is old and unlit. Inside: the motel office, as described.
